find:
The Day of Judgement (Yawm al-Din)

Muslims believe that this life is a test, and that every person will face judgement before Allah at the end of time. The Day of Judgement is described vividly in the Qur’an as a terrifying, earth-shaking event. Surah 99:1–2 states: “When the earth is shaken with its earthquake, and the earth discharges its burdens.”

On this day, the angel Israfil will blow a trumpet, and all living things will die. Then a second blast will resurrect every person who has ever lived. Each person will stand before Allah and their book of deeds — recorded by the angels throughout their life — will be opened. Those who receive their book in the right hand will enter paradise; those who receive it in the left hand will face punishment.

Surah 99:7–8 states: “Whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it. And whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it.” This teaches that no action — however small — escapes Allah’s notice. Every good deed and every sin will be accounted for.

Surah 23:102–103 describes the scales of judgement: “Those whose good deeds weigh heavy will be successful, but those whose balance is light will have lost their souls for ever and will stay in Hell.” Good deeds are weighed against bad deeds, and the balance determines a person’s fate.
note: S2: Day of Judgement is lesson 5 content; section removed, diagram marker kept

find:
Akhirah — Life After Death

Akhirah means life after death. Muslims believe the afterlife is eternal and that this earthly life is merely a temporary test. What a person does in this life determines their fate in the next. This belief underpins Muslim morality — every action carries consequences that extend beyond death.

Jannah (Paradise): The Qur’an describes Jannah as a place of eternal peace, pleasure and closeness to Allah. Surah 47:15 describes rivers of water, milk, wine and honey, with fruits of every kind and forgiveness from Allah. Jannah has multiple levels, with the highest reserved for the most righteous. It is the ultimate reward for those who lived according to Allah’s will.

Jahannam (Hell): Jahannam is a place of torment and punishment for those who rejected Allah or lived sinfully without repentance. The Qur’an describes fire, boiling water and suffering. Surah 4:56 describes how the skin of those in hell will be replaced so they continue to feel the punishment. Most Muslims believe Jahannam can be temporary for sinful Muslims — Allah may forgive them and eventually admit them to paradise — but it is eternal for those who committed Shirk (associating partners with Allah).

Key Fact

Belief in Akhirah means Muslims see this life as a preparation for eternity. Every deed is recorded and will be judged. This motivates Muslims to pray, give charity, avoid sin and follow the Qur’an and Sunnah — because the stakes are not just for this life but for the life to come.

find: Muslims believe that after death, the soul enters Barzakh — a state of waiting between death and the Day of Judgement. In the grave, two angels (Munkar and Nakir) question the deceased about their faith: “Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is your prophet?” A righteous person will answer correctly and experience comfort; a sinful person will struggle and experience suffering. This period lasts until the Day of Resurrection.
replace:
A common misunderstanding is that Al-Qadr hands Muslims an excuse: if Allah has written it, the person cannot be blamed. Muslim teaching rejects that. Allah knowing a choice in advance is not the same as Allah making the choice for someone. The person still weighs up the options and acts, so the action is theirs.

This is why Muslims are still expected to work hard, seek medical treatment, revise for tests and ask forgiveness when they do wrong. Trust in Allah’s plan and personal effort belong together. A well-known saying advises a Muslim to tie up their camel first and then trust in Allah.

Key Fact

Muslims hold two beliefs at the same time: Allah has determined what will happen, and people still choose freely. Because the choice genuinely belongs to the person, that person answers for it. Al-Qadr explains Allah’s power; ikhtiyar explains human responsibility.

Muslims believe this responsibility is finally settled on the Day of Judgement, when every person answers to Allah for the choices they made freely. Al-Qadr and accountability therefore fit together rather than clash. The next lesson covers Akhirah — life after death, the Day of Judgement and what Muslims believe comes after it.

expect.text: Explain two ways in which belief in Akhirah (life after death) influences Muslims today.
expect.marks:
Up to 2 marks for each influence explained:
• Because Muslims believe every deed will be judged, they are motivated to perform good actions such as giving to charity (Zakah), being honest and helping others. The Qur'an says even an 'atom's weight' of good or evil will be seen (Surah 99:7–8).
• Belief in the afterlife gives Muslims comfort when facing death or bereavement. They trust that righteous people will enter Jannah (paradise), which is a place of eternal peace and happiness. This hope reduces the fear of death and encourages patience during suffering.
• Akhirah discourages sinful behaviour because Muslims know that wrongdoing will be punished, either in Jahannam or through the questioning in the grave (Barzakh). This acts as a moral deterrent.
[4 marks]

value.text: Explain two ways in which belief in human responsibility influences Muslims today.
value.marks:
Up to 2 marks for each influence explained:
• Muslims believe they answer for their own actions, so they try to be honest, generous and kind in everyday life. They cannot blame family, friends or fate, because no one carries another person's sins (Surah 17:15).
• Responsibility rules out fatalism. A Muslim who is ill still seeks treatment, and a Muslim who does wrong still asks forgiveness, because effort and trust in Allah's plan belong together.
[4 marks]

expect.text:
'Belief in the afterlife is the most important belief in Islam.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Muslim teachings
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
expect.marks:
Top band (10–12) Well-argued response with reasoned consideration of different points of view, supported by knowledge and religious references.
Upper-mid band (7–9) Reasoned consideration with clear reference to religion.
Lower-mid band (4–6) Reasoned consideration of a point of view. Maximum 6 marks if there is no reference to religion.
Lower band (1–3) Point of view with reason(s) stated.

Arguments supporting:
• Akhirah gives purpose to this life — without belief in the afterlife, there would be less motivation to follow Allah's commands. This life is a test for the next.
• Surah 99:7–8 teaches that every deed, no matter how small, will be accounted for. This underpins all Muslim morality and worship.
• The Day of Judgement is when all other beliefs (Tawhid, prophethood, angels) culminate — it is the ultimate test of faith.

Arguments against:
• Tawhid (oneness of Allah) is the most fundamental belief — it is the first part of the Shahadah and the basis of all other beliefs. Without God, there would be no afterlife.
• Belief in the Qur'an and prophethood could be seen as more important because they provide the guidance Muslims need to pass the test of this life.
• All beliefs are interconnected — the Six Articles and Five Roots work as a complete system. Isolating one as 'most important' misses how they reinforce each other.
• Some Muslims might argue that practical obedience (the Five Pillars) matters more than any single doctrinal belief.
[12 marks]

value.text:
'Predestination means no one is really free.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Muslim teachings
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
value.marks:
Top band (10–12) Both sides argued in depth, religious teaching used throughout, justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (7–9) Both sides argued with clear religious teaching.
Lower-mid band (4–6) One side argued with reasons. Maximum 6 marks without reference to religion.
Low band (1–3) A point of view with a simple reason.

Arguments supporting:
• Al-Qadr teaches that Allah has already determined everything, and Surah 9:51 says only what God has decreed will happen to us.
• An angel records a person's provision, lifespan and deeds before birth, so a life can look settled in advance.
• Sunni teaching stresses that even hardship is part of Allah's plan, which can sound as though people simply receive what is written.

Arguments against:
• Knowing is not causing. Allah knows what a person will choose, but the person still chooses, like a teacher who knows a student will fail without revision.
• Muslims believe in ikhtiyar, genuine freedom of choice, and Surah 17:15 says no one carries another's sins — which only makes sense if the choices are our own.
• Shi'a Muslims stress Adalat, the justice of Allah: it would be unjust to make someone sin and then punish them for it.
• Al-Qadr does not make Muslims passive. They are still expected to work hard, make good choices and seek forgiveness.
[12 marks]
